provenance.title: Not just a digital pedigree. A full chain of provenance.
provenance.intro: When a dog entering the POKIU registry already has a pedigree issued by another organization (e.g. ZKwP, FCI), the system doesn't turn that document into a dead scan in a folder. It builds a documented chain of provenance: original pedigree → verified by POKIU → registered with POKIU → digitally verifiable POKIU pedigree — and shows every link in that chain publicly, on the same page where the pedigree itself gets verified.

timeline.title: Original pedigree
timeline.description: A document issued by another kennel organization — submitted by the breeder or the office.

timeline.title: Verified by POKIU
timeline.description: The office checks the microchip and parents against the source document, manually redacts personal data, and publishes a preview.

timeline.title: Registered with POKIU
timeline.description: The dog enters the POKIU registry with a full reference back to the source document.

timeline.title: Digitally verifiable POKIU pedigree
timeline.description: The issued POKIU pedigree, with a QR code linking to the public chain of provenance.

layers.title: 1. Document attached
layers.description: Whether the original source document is attached to the registration.

layers.title: 2. Consistency with the POKIU registry
layers.description: Whether the microchip and parent data in the source document match the POKIU registry.

layers.title: 3. Source document verification
layers.description: Whether POKIU staff actually verified the document, or only attached it.

layers.title: 4. DNA-confirmed parentage
layers.description: Shown only when a real DNA test result exists — never as a default status.

provenance.exampleQuote: The POKIU document was issued based on a verified source document issued by [organization], number [number].
provenance.buyerQuote: A buyer, breeder, or foreign organization can independently confirm the document's authenticity, its consistency with the registry, and the source of the registered lineage.
disclaimers: Displaying the source document does not mean its original issuer recognizes the POKIU pedigree.
Digital verification is not proof of genetic parentage — only a DNA test confirms parentage, and the system only shows that status when one actually exists.

ksiegai.title: KsięgaI
ksiegai.subtitle: Financial infrastructure for Polish companies — built around KSeF, accountability, and automation.
ksiegai.description: KsięgaI connects invoicing, KSeF, payments, documents, banking, and the company's books in one system. Every company keeps control over its data, access, and decisions — whether the action is taken by the owner, the accountant, an employee, or a connected AI agent.

role.title: Our Own Product, Not Just a Client Build
role.description: Unlike client projects, KsięgaI is a system TOVERNET designs, develops, and maintains as its own product — daily proof that we can build and operate infrastructure under real regulatory pressure (KSeF), not just design it on paper.

problem.title: The Problem Doesn't End When the Invoice Is Issued
problem.description: Issuing an invoice is the easy part. The real problem starts afterward: who approved it, was it sent to the right KSeF environment, did the client pay, was the bank transaction reconciled, did the document reach the books, and who was actually allowed to perform each of those operations.
workflow: Sent to the correct KSeF environment
Payment reconciled against a bank transaction
Every step logged along with who had the right to perform it

ksefArchitecture.title: Every KSeF Operation Has Its Own Level of Responsibility
ksefArchitecture.intro: KSeF isn't "send an XML." The system has to handle authentication and company identity, test and production environments, tokens and certificates, permissions, active sessions, XML generation and parsing, submissions, UPO and status retrieval, errors and retries, incoming-invoice synchronization, and separating the owner's role from the accountant's and everyone else's. Instead of one broad endpoint with one broad permission, each of these operations has its own access level.

cards.title: Token Verification
cards.description: Checks the connection without granting access to any financial operation — available to any signed-in user, before the account is even linked to a company.

cards.title: Credential Management
cards.description: Available only to the company's owner and admin — not to everyone who handles the bookkeeping.

cards.title: Document Synchronization
cards.description: A controlled operation running in the context of one specific company, triggered by a dedicated worker process.

cards.title: Invoice Submission
cards.description: Separated from synchronization and handled by its own dedicated submission process with its own queue.

ksefArchitecture.auditQuote: We didn't consider the implementation correct just because it "worked." We compared it field by field against the official KSeF schema and tested real transitions against the Ministry of Finance's environment.
auditFindings: Incoming invoices from counterparties weren't being reconciled against the register of received documents — a critical defect, fixed before broader production use.
An operator-precedence bug in VAT calculation, plus KSeF rejecting invoices with multiple VAT rates.
A field required by the official XSD schema that was missing.
ksefArchitecture.leakFix: The same verification pass also found a case where one endpoint wasn't scoping its query to the right company — it could theoretically have exposed another company's KSeF token metadata. Found in our own internal audit, confirmed against real data, and fixed before it could be exploited.

permissions.title: Access to a Company Doesn't Mean Access to Everything
permissions.intro: Every company is isolated at the database level — not just hidden by frontend logic. Roles differ in what they can see and what they can do.

roles.sees: Documents and books covered by their role
Only the data available to the person who connected it
roles.canDo: Only permitted MCP operations, within its assigned permission tier

permissions.mainSentence: An AI agent's permissions aren't a separate "superaccess" tier. The agent operates exactly within the bounds of the person and company that connected it — at one of several permission tiers, from read-only to full posting.
permissions.isolationNote: Every organization is isolated by a company identifier and database-level access rules — over 700 such rules across the system, not a single exception.

mcp.title: AI That Can Work on the Books — But Can't Bypass Permissions
mcp.intro: KsięgaI has a dedicated MCP server that AI assistants can connect to (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and other compatible clients). The agent doesn't get its own, broader access to the database — it operates exactly within the permissions of the person who connected it, at one of several defined access tiers.
mcp.example: An AI agent was asked to analyze a company's accounts for a given month. On its own, it compared issued invoices, payment statuses, bank transactions, imported expenses, the posting queue, and the journal entries. It then flagged unpaid invoices, unposted documents, and discrepancies needing action.
mcp.examplesTitle: What You Can Ask It To Do
examples: Compare the bank against the books and explain the differences.
Add this expense invoice from a photo.
Show KSeF documents that were downloaded but never posted.
mcp.safetyNote: New journal entries and bank postings created by the agent land as drafts — never auto-approved. Approval stays with a human.
mcp.closingSentence: The same interface can run in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, or any other compatible MCP client. The company decides who connects their agent and what access tier it gets.

banking.title: The Bank Isn't a Separate Island
items: Bank infrastructure built to add further providers
Original imported data retained for audit purposes
Duplicate detection when the same file is imported again
A separate posting queue instead of silently altering the existing ledger
banking.mismatchTitle: When a Statement Doesn't Match the Account
banking.mismatchNote: If an imported statement looks like it came from a different account or currency than expected, the system doesn't quietly try to "make it fit." The import is flagged for manual review instead of being silently posted. In a financial system, a visible warning beats a convenient-looking but wrong match.

accounting.title: Accounting as a Controlled State Machine
accounting.intro: A document doesn't just "appear" in the books. First it arrives, then it's analyzed, reconciled, approved — and only then does it become a journal entry.
accounting.modulesTitle: The Modules That Make This Up
accounting.queueNote: An imported document first lands in a posting queue awaiting review. Only an approved queue item becomes an actual journal entry — and old entries are never hard-deleted, only marked voided along with a reason.

branches.title: Next Direction: Safe Accounting Variants
branches.description: We're working on a model inspired by version-control systems: an accountant can prepare an alternative posting or chart-of-accounts variant on an isolated branch, compare its effects, and only then approve merging it into the real books.
uses: Reviewing before posting to the main books
Keeping an exact history of proposed and accepted changes
branches.status: In research and development — not yet a finished production feature.

eventLog.title: Event and Decision Trail
eventLog.description: KsięgaI records not just the current result but the business meaning of an operation: who performed it, in what context, what it concerned, and what caused it. Every KSeF submission attempt lands in an immutable submission log — whether or not it succeeded.
eventLog.supports: This supports auditability, safer automation, and explaining why the system reached a given state — without letting AI directly edit the database tables.
eventLog.aiNote: AI issues a business command — it doesn't edit the database.

migration.title: Rebuilding Working Infrastructure Without Guessing
migration.description: As the system grew, individual Supabase Edge Functions were replaced with a shared API gateway and shared pipelines. The migration preserved the existing request/response contracts, so the application could evolve its architecture without rewriting the whole product at once — the old and new paths worked identically during the transition.
migration.findingsTitle: What We Found Along the Way
findings: A dead function that was still logging raw KSeF tokens — removed before anyone could use it.
A forgotten endpoint acting as an open, unauthenticated proxy — closed during the same review.
migration.closing: Old functions weren't just deleted — they were archived ("_legacy") along with a note explaining why they stopped being used. That's the same discipline that lets us safely rebuild a client's running system instead of only building demos from scratch.

security.title: Security Isn't a Separate Module
security.philosophy: Every operation is evaluated by who's performing it, for which company, on what basis, and whether it requires re-confirming identity.
points: KSeF test and production environments kept separate
Rate limiting at the API gateway level, stricter for authentication operations
The admin panel is completely separated from the rest of the system and not publicly reachable
Narrow, individually-granted permissions instead of one universal access key
Regular internal audits that actually find and close defects — not just on paper

builtByOperating.title: Built By Running Our Own Companies
builtByOperating.description: KsięgaI wasn't built from a feature list drawn up by a software house. We develop it while running our own companies — issuing real invoices, importing real bank statements, handling KSeF, and working with real accountants. Tovernet was, and is, its own first and most demanding user — every broken workflow immediately hit a real business process, not just a test environment.

ksiegai.storyLine: We started with an invoicing program and built a controlled operating layer for the whole company — connecting documents, accounting, banking, KSeF, and AI agents in one model of accountability.

problem.title: You're paying every month. You have no way to check what for.
problem.text: Plenty of businesses sign a contract with an SEO agency, a software house, or an IT freelancer, pay invoices month after month — and don't have the technical knowledge or time to check whether the work is actually happening, whether they still control their own website and domain, and whether what they see in a report matches reality. Tovernet steps into that gap as an independent, technical third party — with no stake in protecting the vendor.

legalBoundary.line1: Tovernet is not a law firm and doesn't provide legal services. Our role is to deliver reliable technical documentation and facts — further decisions, including legal ones, are made by the client together with their own chosen lawyer.
legalBoundary.line2: We don't rule on the legality of a vendor's conduct, don't represent the client in proceedings, and don't guarantee recovery of funds. If a case requires legal escalation, the material we prepare goes to the client's legal counsel as supporting documentation.

faq.q: How is a Tovernet audit different from legal advice?
faq.a: We're not a law firm. We handle the technical side: what was actually delivered, who has access to what, whether invoices match reality. Legal questions are left to the client's own lawyer.

faq.q: How much does an audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the scope and complexity of the case — we don't have a fixed price list. The initial assessment, where we scope the work, is always free.

faq.q: Does Tovernet contact my vendor directly?
faq.a: Only with your explicit consent and within an agreed scope. By default we work for the client only, based on available documents and access.

faq.q: Can the report be used in court?
faq.a: The report is technical documentation, not a court-appointed expert opinion. It can serve as supporting material for a lawyer — how it's used is a decision for the counsel handling the case.

faq.q: What if I don't have access to my own website or domain?
faq.a: That's a common starting point. The first step is establishing what technically exists and what a realistic recovery path looks like.

faq.q: Do you guarantee getting my money back?
faq.a: No. We establish the facts and provide an estimated market value for the delivered work — financial and legal decisions remain the client's.

faq.q: How long does an audit take?
faq.a: It depends on scope — from a few days for a simple check to a few weeks for a complex case spanning multiple systems and contracts.
Yes. Materials and findings go to the client only, unless they decide otherwise.

faq.q: Do you only check SEO agencies?
faq.a: No — we also cover software houses, IT freelancers, hosting and domain providers, and CRM/ERP/CMS vendors.

faq.q: What if my vendor isn't doing anything wrong?
faq.a: That's a valuable outcome too. An audit sometimes confirms the relationship is working correctly — that peace of mind is worth as much as catching a problem.
